title: Our method in each style
teaches: The same steps run every trade, day, swing or position: find the setup, set the stop, size from it, manage it, review it, under our 2% ceiling. What changes with the clock is the chart you read, where the stop sits and so the size, and whether you carry gaps overnight.

walkthroughs.title: Same steps, any clock
steps: Every trade runs the same steps. Find the setup, set the stop, size from it, manage it, review it.
A day trade opens and closes the same day. A position trade can run for months.
What changes is the chart you read, where the stop sits, and so the size.

walkthroughs.title: What our rules set
steps: Our risk on any trade is 0.25% to 2% of the account. 2% is the hard ceiling.
Our default stop is the low of the day, or the prior day's low.
Each setup plan has its own stop. Our trims, a third at 3R and at 5R, are measured from it.

walkthroughs.title: What changes with the clock
steps: A short-term trader buying near the open might put the stop under the low of the first 10 minutes.
A longer-term trader judges exits on a longer timeframe, so the stop sits farther away.
Same risk, wider stop, smaller position. The size moves; the risk doesn't.

questions.q: You move from swing trades to day trades. Which part of your trade plan can you drop?
choices: None: every part stays in the plan
The size, it's only a few hours
The exit, out by the close
questions.answer: None: every part stays in the plan
questions.why: None of them. Schwab's day-trading page says a day trader still plans when to enter and exit, how much to risk, and what to trade. Only the clock is shorter. Watching the screen is not a stop. Our rule is a real stop order with the broker, not one kept in your head. Being out by the close is a deadline, not an exit price.
questions.lesson_line: A shorter hold is no reason for a thinner plan.

wrong.The stop, you'll be watching: Watching isn't a stop. Our rule is a real stop order with the broker, and a fast market can fill below your price.
wrong.The size, it's only a few hours: Size is what caps the loss. Shares come from the dollars you'll risk over the distance to the stop.
wrong.The exit, out by the close: The close is a deadline, not an exit plan. You still need the price that says you're wrong.

questions.simple: None of them, because a day trade still needs a stop, a size and an exit, just over less time.

reasons: fixed before (key reworded by the checker)

questions.q: Our 2% ceiling on risk per trade can stretch on a day trade, since you're out by the close.
questions.why: False. 2% is our hard ceiling on risk per trade, in every style. Our risk runs 0.25% to 2% of the account. It is chosen by setup quality, your recent results, market conditions and your edge. How long you hold is not on that list. Being out by the close doesn't cap the loss either. A fast market can fill a stop well below its price.
questions.lesson_line: One ceiling for every style: 2% of the account per trade.
questions.simple: False, because 2% is our hard ceiling on every trade, and a short hold does not raise it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A1, 2% ceiling)

questions.q: Day trade or position trade, what order do the steps go in?
questions.why: Setup, stop, size, manage, review. Find the setup first. Put the stop where the idea fails. Measure the distance from entry to stop, and size last. Schwab's worked example divides the dollars you'll risk by that distance. After you close, review the trade. Closing isn't the final step.
questions.lesson_line: The order never changes. Only the clock does.

wrong.Setup, size, stop, manage, review: Size before stop is the mistake StockCharts calls the biggest. The distance to the stop is what sets the size.
wrong.Size, setup, stop, manage, review: A size picked before there's even a setup leaves the stop to be bent around it.
wrong.Stop, setup, size, manage, review: The stop goes where the idea fails, so you need the setup first. A stop picked before the chart isn't tied to anything.

questions.simple: Setup, then stop, then size, then manage, then review, because the size comes from how far away the stop is.

reasons: fixed before (f19 added by the checker)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits.
questions.sentence: Same stock, same risk, wider stop: the position gets ___.
questions.why: Smaller. Shares are the dollars you'll risk divided by the distance to the stop. Move the stop farther away and the same risk buys fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: The chart sets the stop. The stop sets the size.

questions.q: Two trades share the same entry and stop. Their 3R price is the same, even if one is held longer.
questions.why: True. R is your risk per share: the entry minus the stop. So 3R is a price, not a date. Same entry and same stop give the same 3R price, however long you hold. When you sell is a judgment, and he usually waits until day 3 at the earliest. Change the stop and 3R moves with it.
questions.lesson_line: R marks are measured from the stop, not from the calendar.
questions.simple: True, because the 3R price comes from the entry and the stop, not from how long you hold.

deeper.trap: The catch is the stop, not the clock. Longer holds often use wider stops, and a wider stop pushes 3R farther from the entry. This question fixes the entry and the stop, so the 3R price matches. Change the stop and the price moves with it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: You time our Go Signal entry on the 30-minute chart. Where does the stop go?
questions.why: Just under the session's low. The Go Signal plan buys the prior close when it trades that session, else the close. Its stop is the session's low. Our stops sit a few cents under the low, not exactly on it. The real trigger shows on the 30 or 65-minute chart. Timing the entry there doesn't move the stop onto that clock.
questions.lesson_line: An intraday entry can still carry a daily stop. The Go Signal's is the low of the day.

wrong.Just under the prior close: That's the entry level, so it leaves almost no room. The plan's stop is the session's low.
wrong.A flat 10% under your entry: That isn't the Go Signal plan. Its stop is a chart level: the session's low.
wrong.Under the latest 30-minute bar: That puts the stop on the entry's clock. The plan's stop is the session's low.

questions.simple: Just under the session's low, because the Go Signal keeps its daily stop when you time the buy on a 30-minute chart.

reasons: rests on house plans (TRADE_PLANS.md Go Signal) and the rulebook (F62)
key reworded for length balance and F62

questions.q: A day trader dodges overnight gaps, so a day trade's stop fills right at the stop price.
questions.why: False. The stop price is a trigger, not a guaranteed price. Once hit, the stop becomes a market order. In a fast market it can fill well below the stop, even in the middle of the day. Dodging overnight gaps removes one risk, not this one.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger, not a guaranteed price, in every style.
questions.simple: False, because a stop only triggers a market order, and in a fast market that order can fill well below the stop.

deeper.trap: A short intraday drop can trigger a stop and fill it far below where the stock closes that day. So a day trader can lose more than planned with no gap at all. The SEC calls the stop price a trigger, not the execution price.

questions.q: You trade more than one style. Which of these changes from style to style?
questions.why: Where your stop sits. Know your timeframe for every trade. A short-term trader buying near the open might use the low of the first 10 minutes. A longer-term trader judges exits on a longer timeframe, and might trail 10% below. The 2% ceiling, the written plan and the review stay the same. A different stop means a different size for the same risk.
questions.lesson_line: Know your timeframe for every trade. It decides where the stop goes.

wrong.Our 2% risk ceiling: That one never moves. 2% is our hard ceiling on any trade.
wrong.Having a written plan: Every style needs one. A day trader's plan sets the same things: when in, when out, how much to risk.
wrong.Reviewing your trades: Every style ends with a review. Closing the trade isn't the final step.

questions.simple: Where your stop sits changes with the timeframe, while the 2% ceiling, the plan and the review stay put.

questions.q: A day trade in a $50,000 account: entry $18.60, stop $18.35, just under the first 10-minute low. You'll risk $200. How many shares?
questions.why: 800 shares. Shares are the dollars you'll risk divided by the distance from entry to stop. Here that is $200 over $18.60 minus $18.35. Our rule then caps any position at 40% of the account, and 800 shares at $18.60 stays under it. It's the same formula as a swing trade.
questions.lesson_line: Day trade or swing trade: shares are dollars at risk over risk per share.
questions.simple: 800 shares, because you divide the $200 you risk by the gap between your entry and your stop.

reasons: fixed before (stem reworded by the checker)

questions.q: Several of our setup plans trail under the 10-day or 21-day average. Which of these gives the best read on a hold of up to a year?
questions.why: The 200-day average. The average you read should fit how long you hold. Schwab says a position trader willing to hold up to a year gets a better read from the 200-day. ChartSchool says long-term investors often use 100 or more periods. We use the 200-day too: no longs below it, unless it is a parabolic long. It is a line we read, not our trail. Our setup plans still trail under the 10-day or 21-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Same rule, longer clock: the average you watch should fit how long you hold.

wrong.The 10-day average: Schwab ties the 10 and 20-day to holds of 10 trading days or less. It hugs price and turns quickly, too fast for a hold of up to a year.
wrong.The 21-day average: ChartSchool puts 20 to 60 periods with medium-term trends. A hold of up to a year calls for a longer one.
wrong.The 100-hour average: That is 100 periods, but of hourly bars. A longer-term trader judges exits on a longer timeframe, not intraday levels.

questions.simple: The 200-day, because a long hold needs a long average, and Schwab says it reads best for holds up to a year.

deeper.counter: Not every long-term trader uses the 200-day. ChartSchool only says long-term investors often use 100 or more periods. The point is the match: a short average for a short hold, a long one for a long hold.

reasons: touches the rulebook's E52 trail (owner flag)

questions.q: A Go Signal: price trades through $40.00, the prior close, and you buy. Stop $39.20. What price is 3R?
questions.why: $42.40. R is your risk per share: the $40.00 entry minus the $39.20 stop. 3R adds three times that distance to the entry. It is a measuring mark, not an order to sell. When you sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later.
questions.lesson_line: 3R is three times your risk per share, added to the entry.
questions.simple: $42.40, because you add three times your risk per share, the entry minus the stop, to the $40.00 entry.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
fixed before (2R target moved to 3R trim)

questions.story: You plan a position trade in a US company's stock. You expect to hold it for about six months.
questions.q: What must this plan cover that a day trade plan can skip?
choices: Which hourly bar to buy on
questions.why: Whether to sit through reports. A US company files a 10-Q for each of its first three fiscal quarters, and a 10-K for the year. A six-month hold spans more than one quarter. News outside trading hours can gap a stock past your stop. In Fidelity's example a stop at 95 sold near 90 after an overnight gap. Our rule: hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. A day trade closes the same day, so it has no hold-or-sell call to make. Our rule still bars any new buy in the 3 days before a report.
questions.lesson_line: A long hold sits through quarterly reports. Decide what you'll do at each one before you buy.

wrong.The first 10-minute low: That's a short-term stop for a trade near the open. A months-long hold judges exits on a longer timeframe.
wrong.Which hourly bar to buy on: Every trade decides when to enter, in any style. Your entry bar does nothing when a report gaps the stock.
wrong.Nothing, the stop covers it: A gap can jump the stop. In Fidelity's example a stop at 95 sold near 90 after an overnight gap.

questions.simple: Whether to sit through reports, because a six-month hold spans reports that can gap the stock past your stop.

reasons: fixed before (story gave the key away)

questions.q: A position trader who makes only a few trades a year can skip reviewing them.
questions.why: False. Closing out a trade isn't the final step. You still evaluate the results. Record your trades in a journal. Our rule is to journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally. Whatever the method, keep good records so you can track your progress.
questions.lesson_line: Every style ends the same way: log the trade and review it.
questions.simple: False, because every style ends with a review, and even a few trades a year need records to track your progress.

questions.story: You hold two swing trades and have new buys planned this week. Then the general market turns weak, and most stocks are falling.
questions.q: What's the right move?
choices: Take fewer new trades for now
Ignore it, the stock is what counts
Widen your stops to ride it out
Buy more, prices are lower now
questions.answer: Take fewer new trades for now
questions.why: Take fewer new trades. A market filter decides when our account trades. As the market weakens, our guide is fewer and smaller trades, and mostly cash at the worst. Hirsch's answer to a bearish turn also starts with limiting new buys. Your open trades keep their stops, which only move up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: When the general market turns weak, take fewer new trades. Don't trade against it.

wrong.Ignore it, the stock is what counts: A market filter decides when our account trades. Swing traders track the broader market so they aren't trading against it.
wrong.Widen your stops to ride it out: That adds risk just as the market turns against you. Our stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Buy more, prices are lower now: Our rule is one buy at one price, with no adding. Hirsch warns buying more of a falling stock can lose money fast.

questions.simple: Take fewer new trades, because our market filter calls for fewer trades when the general market turns weak.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A1 market conditions, A4 stop only moves up)

questions.q: Jeffrey Hirsch allows stops up to 20%, but no position may lose over 2% of the portfolio. With a 20% stop, how big can the position be?
questions.why: 10% of the portfolio. Divide the 2% loss cap by the 20% stop. A 10% position that falls 20% loses 2% of the portfolio. A wide long-term stop fits the cap because the position is sized down to match. This is Hirsch's practice, not our stop. Our stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A wide stop on a long hold is fine. The size shrinks so the risk doesn't grow.
questions.simple: 10% of the portfolio, because a 20% stop on a 10% position loses 2% of the portfolio, inside Hirsch's cap.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the 20% as a stop to copy. It is Hirsch's outer limit for a longer-term portfolio, paired with a small position. A 20% stop on a big position breaks the 2% cap fast. Our own stops usually sit within about 3% of the buy.

questions.story: Your day trade is up 2R at 3:45 p.m. and closing strong. You sized it for a tight intraday stop. No earnings are due, and you'd like to hold it a few days.
questions.q: If you hold it overnight, what has to change?
choices: New plan: daily stop, new size
Keep the size, stop to breakeven
Keep the intraday stop and size
questions.answer: New plan: daily stop, new size
questions.why: New plan: daily stop, new size. The trade was built for one day, with a stop for intraday moves. For a hold of days, I'd use our default stop. That is a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low. A wider stop means a smaller size for the same risk. So sell part of it into strength until the size fits. A tight stop never justifies a big position, because a gap can jump the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Change the clock and you re-run the steps: new stop, new size.

wrong.Nothing, it's already working: The plan was built for one day. News after the close can gap it, and the stop was set for intraday moves.
wrong.Keep the size, stop to breakeven: A breakeven stop can't catch an overnight gap, and the size was built for a tight intraday stop. A gap down at that size costs far more than planned.
wrong.Keep the intraday stop and size: A tight intraday stop sits inside a normal day's swings, so a hold of days can get stopped out early. It can't catch an overnight gap either.

questions.simple: Make a new plan with our default daily stop, because a wider stop means a smaller size for the same risk.

deeper.trap: The trap is that a winner feels safe. Being up 2R at 3:45 p.m. says nothing about tonight's news. The size came from a tight intraday stop. An overnight gap at that size can cost far more than the plan allowed. Re-run the steps as if it were a new trade: stop first, then size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (default stop, F62, A7)

questions.story: Two traders own the same stock. It pulls back to its 50-day average, and the long uptrend is intact. The swing trader's stop is hit. The position trader's stop sits lower and isn't touched.
questions.q: Who broke their plan?
questions.why: Neither. Each stop sits on its own timeframe. A position trader sits through pullbacks while the trend holds. A swing trader trades the smaller swings inside the longer move. The swing trader's stop was hit, so selling was the plan. The position trader's stop wasn't touched, so holding was the plan. Judge each trade by its own plan.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out on one clock can be noise on a longer one. Judge each trade by its own plan.

wrong.The position trader, for holding: That stop sits on a longer timeframe, and this pullback didn't reach it. Holding is the plan.
wrong.The swing trader, for selling: Taking the stop was the plan. Holding past it would have been the mistake.
wrong.Both, the stops should match: Different holds need different stops. Matching them would put one trader on the wrong clock.

questions.simple: Neither, because each trader followed a stop set for their own timeframe, and a pullback can hit one without the other.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging one plan by the other's result. If the stock turns back up, the swing trader may feel wrong for selling. If it keeps falling, the position trader may feel wrong for holding. Neither feeling means a plan was broken. A plan is broken when you skip your own stop or rule.

questions.story: You buy our Kicker at $50.00. The Kicker candle's low is $47.00.
questions.q: Where does our stop go?
questions.why: $48.25, 3.5% under entry. Our Kicker stop goes under the Kicker's low, or 3.5% under the entry if that is closer. 3.5% under $50.00 is $48.25. The candle's low at $47.00 is farther away, so the 3.5% stop wins. On a Kicker whose low is the closer one, the stop goes under the low instead.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker stop: under the Kicker's low, or 3.5% under entry, whichever is closer.

wrong.$45.00, 10% under entry: A flat 10% isn't in the Kicker plan. The rule is the candle's low or 3.5%, whichever is closer.
wrong.Just under the $47.00 low: That's the other half of the rule. 3.5% under entry is closer here, so it wins.
wrong.$48.50, 3% under entry: Close, but the Kicker plan names 3.5%, not 3%. 3.5% under $50.00 is $48.25.

questions.simple: $48.25, because the Kicker stop takes whichever is closer to entry, and 3.5% under $50.00 is closer than $47.00.

deeper.trap: The trap is picking the candle's low because it looks like the natural stop. On a big Kicker candle the low can sit far below the entry. The rule takes the closer of the two, so the 3.5% half caps how far below the entry the stop can sit.

reasons: rests on house plans (TRADE_PLANS.md Kicker row)

questions.story: Your day trades put 25% of the account in, with stops 2% under entry. You switch to position trades, keep 25% positions, and set stops 10% under.
questions.q: What's the problem?
choices: Risk is now 2.5%, over our ceiling
Risk fell, the stop is farther away
Risk is now 10%, same as the stop
questions.answer: Risk is now 2.5%, over our ceiling
questions.why: Risk is now 2.5%, over our ceiling. Risk is size times stop distance: 25% times 10% is 2.5% of the account. 2% is our hard ceiling. The stop went from 2% to 10%, and the size didn't move. To stay at or under 2%, shrink the size to fit the wider stop.
questions.lesson_line: Switch to wider stops and the size must shrink. Never carry your old size onto a new clock.

wrong.None, the size didn't change: The size is the problem. Risk is size times stop distance, and the stop went from 2% to 10%.
wrong.Risk fell, the stop is farther away: A farther stop means more loss per share. With the same size, the risk goes up, not down.
wrong.Risk is now 10%, same as the stop: 10% is the loss on the position, not the account. Risk is size times stop: 25% times 10% is 2.5%.

questions.simple: Risk is now 2.5%, because a 25% position with a 10% stop risks 2.5%, over our 2% ceiling.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking the position size alone is the risk. The 25% position fit the ceiling with a 2% stop. With a 10% stop it breaks it. Change the stop and you must re-run the size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A1 ceiling, size times stop)

questions.story: A day trade. Your stop is 0.25% under entry, at the low of the first few minutes. You risk 1% of the account, as on your swing trades.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Widen the stop to shrink the size
questions.why: Cap the size. 1% risk over a 0.25% stop works out to 400% of the account. Risk per trade and position size are two separate limits. Our max position is 40% of the account. A tight stop never justifies more, because a gap can jump the stop. So the size is the smaller of the risk-based size and the cap.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop doesn't license a giant position. Cap the size.

wrong.Buy the full 400%, on margin: A small price move the wrong way can wipe out a big part of the account. And a fast market can fill a stop well below it.
wrong.Widen the stop to shrink the size: The stop belongs where the idea fails. Moving it to fix the size gets it backwards; adjust the position instead.
wrong.Tighten the stop even further: A tighter stop makes the formula's size even bigger, and normal swings hit it sooner.

questions.simple: Cap the size, because 1% risk over a 0.25% stop works out to 400% of the account, far past our 40% cap.

deeper.trap: The trap is trusting the formula past its limits. A tight stop makes the formula's size huge, but a stop is only a trigger. A gap or a fast market can fill it well below. At 400% of the account, that loss is many times the 1% you planned.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7 40% cap)

questions.q: By our own rule, which style do our trades use?
choices: Swing trades: days to a few weeks
Day trades, closed by the bell
Position trades up to a year
A new style for each trade
questions.answer: Swing trades: days to a few weeks
questions.simple: Swing trades, because our rule is to hold for days to a few weeks, longer only while a winner keeps working.
questions.why: Swing trades. Our rule: we swing trade, holding for days to a few weeks. A winner can be held longer while it keeps working. The steps in this unit still run the same way in any style.
questions.lesson_line: We swing trade: days to a few weeks, longer only while a winner keeps working.

wrong.Day trades, closed by the bell: A day trade opens and closes the same day. Our rule is to swing trade, for days to a few weeks.
wrong.Position trades up to a year: Our rule says days to a few weeks. A winner may run longer, but only while it keeps working.
wrong.A new style for each trade: Our rule names one style. We swing trade, and a winner can be held longer while it keeps working.

questions.q: Under our rule, deciding to hold a winner longer is no reason to widen its stop.
questions.simple: True, because our stop only moves up, never down or wider, and a longer hold does not change that.
questions.why: True. Our stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is a gap against the stop, not a change of plan. A longer hold is managed by trailing the rising averages.
questions.lesson_line: Our stop only moves up. A longer hold is no reason to widen it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B20 exception)
